config.title: React Router Basics

intro.title: React Router Basics
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple Angular application with multiple views using the Angular Router. You will learn how to set up routing to navigate between different components, such as a home page and an about page, without reloading the entire application. The core concept involves configuring routes, using router directives in templates, and handling navigation programmatically. You will work with key Angular constructs like RouterModule, routes array, router-outlet, and routerLink to create a seamless user experience.
intro.usecase: In Angular applications, routing is essential for creating single-page applications (SPAs) with multiple views, similar to how modern web apps like Gmail or Trello function. Developers use Angular Router to manage navigation between different sections such as user profiles, dashboards, settings panels, and product listings without full page reloads. This pattern enables seamless user experiences in e-commerce sites where customers browse categories, view product details, and proceed to checkout through distinct routes. Understanding routing fundamentals allows you to build maintainable applications with clear navigation structures and lazy-loaded modules for optimal performance.

objectives: Configure a basic routing module in an Angular application
Implement route definitions for different components in the application
Integrate the router outlet directive to render routed components
Apply router links to navigate between different views
Construct a navigation component with router link bindings
Initialize and manipulate route parameters to pass data between components
Control navigation behavior using programmatic routing methods

steps.title: Import RouterModule and Routes from @angular/router
steps.instruction: Import RouterModule and Routes from '@angular/router' in your AppModule or routing module.
steps.hint: Use the import statement with curly braces to bring in both RouterModule and Routes from the '@angular/router' package.
steps.seedCode: // Import RouterModule and Routes from '@angular/router' here
steps.expectedOutcome: The RouterModule and Routes are imported, enabling routing setup in your Angular application.
successCriteria: RouterModule and Routes are imported from '@angular/router'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're importing both RouterModule and Routes from '@angular/router'.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look right. You need to import RouterModule and Routes from '@angular/router' to enable routing.

steps.title: Create route configuration array
steps.instruction: Create a constant named 'routes' of type 'Routes[]' that contains at least two route objects. Each route object should have 'path' and 'component' properties.
steps.hint: Define the routes array after your imports. Use the Routes type you imported. Each route object should specify a path (string) and component (Angular component class).
steps.seedCode:
import { RouterModule, Routes } from '@angular/router';

// Create your routes array here
steps.expectedOutcome: A routes array is defined with at least two route objects, each containing path and component properties.
successCriteria: The code contains a 'routes' constant of type 'Routes[]' with at least two route objects that have both 'path' and 'component' properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your routes array has the correct type annotation and contains at least two complete route objects with both path and component properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: The routes array isn't properly defined. Remember to create a constant named 'routes' of type 'Routes[]' with at least two route objects, each containing path and component properties.

steps.title: Import components for routing
steps.instruction: Import the HomeComponent and AboutComponent from their respective files so they can be used in your routes configuration.
steps.hint: Use the import statement with the component name and the path to its TypeScript file.
steps.expectedOutcome: The HomeComponent and AboutComponent are imported and ready to be referenced in the routes configuration.
successCriteria: HomeComponent and AboutComponent are imported from './home/home.component' and './about/about.component' respectively.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've imported at least one component, but make sure to import both HomeComponent and AboutComponent.
steps.feedbackWrong: The components aren't imported correctly. Check the import syntax and file paths.

steps.title: Configure RouterModule with routes
steps.instruction: In the imports array of your AppModule or routing module, add RouterModule.forRoot(routes) to register your routes.
steps.hint: Add RouterModule.forRoot(routes) to the imports array where you configure your module.
steps.expectedOutcome: The RouterModule is configured with your routes array using forRoot(), enabling routing in your Angular application.
successCriteria: RouterModule.forRoot(routes) is added to the imports array of the module.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're adding RouterModule.forRoot(routes) to the imports array.
steps.feedbackWrong: That's not quite right. You need to add RouterModule.forRoot(routes) to the imports array to register your routes.

steps.title: Add router outlet to main template
steps.instruction: In your app.component.html file, add the <router-outlet></router-outlet> element where routed components should appear.
steps.hint: The router-outlet element acts as a placeholder that Angular will replace with the component matching the current route.
steps.analogousExample:
<!-- In Angular, router-outlet marks where routed content goes -->
<router-outlet></router-outlet>
steps.expectedOutcome: The app.component.html file should contain a <router-outlet> element that will display routed components.
successCriteria: The app.component.html file contains a <router-outlet></router-outlet> element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've added the complete <router-outlet></router-outlet> element to app.component.html.
steps.feedbackWrong: The router outlet element is missing. Add <router-outlet></router-outlet> to app.component.html to create a placeholder for routed content.

steps.title: Create navigation links with routerLink
steps.instruction: In your component's template, add anchor tags with routerLink directives pointing to your route paths. For example, create a navigation bar with links to '/home' and '/about'.
steps.hint: Use the routerLink directive in your anchor tags to create navigation links that work with Angular Router.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have created navigation links that use Angular's routerLink directive to navigate between routes.
successCriteria: Anchor tags with routerLink directives are added to the template, pointing to valid route paths.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using the routerLink directive correctly in your anchor tags and pointing to valid route paths.
steps.feedbackWrong: It looks like the navigation links aren't quite right. Remember to use the routerLink directive in your anchor tags and specify the route paths you want to navigate to.

steps.title: Add routerLinkActive for active styling
steps.instruction: Add the routerLinkActive directive to your existing navigation links to apply CSS classes when the route is active.
steps.hint: Add routerLinkActive='active' to each <a> tag that already has routerLink.
steps.expectedOutcome: The navigation links will have routerLinkActive='active' added to them, enabling automatic CSS class application for active routes.
successCriteria: Both navigation links have routerLinkActive='active' attribute added.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added routerLinkActive to some links, but make sure both navigation links have this directive.
steps.feedbackWrong: The routerLinkActive directive wasn't properly added. Check that you've added routerLinkActive='active' to both <a> tags.

steps.title: Create a default/fallback route
steps.instruction: Add a wildcard route (**) to your routes array that redirects to the Home component when an unknown path is accessed.
steps.hint: In Angular, you can add a route with path: '**' and redirectTo: '/home' to handle unknown routes.
steps.expectedOutcome: Your routes array should now include a wildcard route that redirects unknown paths to the Home component.
successCriteria: The routes array contains a route object with path: '**' and redirectTo: '/home'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your wildcard route has both 'path' and 'redirectTo' properties correctly configured.
steps.feedbackWrong: The wildcard route wasn't added correctly. Check that you're adding it to the routes array with the proper syntax.

steps.title: Add route parameters to a route
steps.instruction: Add a new route with a parameter segment to your routes configuration array. Use the path pattern 'user/:id' and map it to a UserComponent.
steps.hint: In your routes array, add an object with path: 'user/:id' and component: UserComponent. The colon indicates a dynamic parameter.
steps.expectedOutcome: Your routes configuration will include a dynamic route that can match URLs like /user/123 or /user/abc.
successCriteria: The routes array contains a route object with path: 'user/:id' and component: UserComponent.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've added a route with path: 'user/:id' and component: UserComponent to your routes array.
steps.feedbackWrong: The parameterized route wasn't added correctly. Check that you've added { path: 'user/:id', component: UserComponent } to your routes array.

steps.title: Access route parameters in component
steps.instruction: In the UserComponent class, inject ActivatedRoute and use the paramMap observable to access the 'id' parameter from the route.
steps.hint: Import ActivatedRoute from '@angular/router', inject it in the constructor, and subscribe to paramMap to get the parameter value.
steps.expectedOutcome: The UserComponent will be able to retrieve and use the 'id' parameter from the route URL.
successCriteria: ActivatedRoute is injected in the constructor, and paramMap is subscribed to access the 'id' parameter.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're subscribing to paramMap and accessing the 'id' parameter correctly.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you've imported ActivatedRoute, injected it in the constructor, and subscribed to paramMap to get the 'id' parameter.
